extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and advanced law students
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards governing what acts constitute infringement of a U.S. patent (making, using, selling) as applied to machines, manufactures, and compositions; includes doctrines on intent, constructive use, sales of products/materials, territorial assignments, and evidentiary considerations for injunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory grant of exclusive rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute grants the patentee, for a term, "the full and exclusive right and liberty of making, using, and vending to others to be used, the invention or discovery," and gives a right of action for damages in case of "making, using, or selling" the thing patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory wording is the baseline: infringement is tied to the enumerated acts (make/use/sell). Judicial interpretation determines how those terms apply to different subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: General test for infringement (copying without material variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: An infringement takes place whenever a party avails himself of the invention of the patentee, without such variation as will constitute a new discovery; alternatively, an infringement is a copy made after and agreeing with the principle laid down in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus is on whether the accused device/practice appropriates the patentee's invention in substance and effect, not mere immaterial formal differences (citing Walton v. Potter, Galloway v. Bleaden). Courts compare specifications and practical effect to determine if variation is substantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation varies by subject-matter: making/using/vending applied contextually
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute's phrases 'making, using, and vending to others to be used' are to be construed according to the nature of the subject-matter covered by the patent (machine vs. manufacture vs. composition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate what 'making', 'using', and 'selling' mean in light of whether the patent covers a machine, a manufacture, or a composition of matter; the modes of infringement differ by class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making a patented machine: intent-to-use/for-sale requirement (experiment exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a patented machine can be an infringement, but historically courts have treated making as an infringement only when the machine was made 'for use or for sale' (i.e., with intent to profit or to deprive the patentee), whereas making for mere philosophical experiment or to test the specification is not an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the 'intent to use/for sale' test (Whittemore v. Cutter and later cases). Determine whether the maker intended to use the machine commercially or merely to experiment; where intent to infringe exists, making alone imports damage and supports liability (nominal damages if necessary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a patented machine: direct and constructive use
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'using' of a patented machine is proved when the party charged has used it personally, has employed others to use it for him, or has profited by its use; constructive use may arise (e.g., hiring it out or arrangements from which defendant profits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look beyond literal operation to arrangements and benefits: hiring the machine out, owning it and permitting others to operate it for the defendant's benefit, or profiting from its operation can establish 'use' (citing Woodworth v. Hall and Keplinger v. De Young). Courts may treat agents/workmen aiding the use as principals (qui facit per alium facit per se).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability from contractual/purchase arrangements tied to use
rubrics_metrics.description: A party who contracts to purchase the output of a manufacturer using a patented machine may be liable for infringement if the contract is not bona fide but is used to cloak ownership, hiring, or control of the machine (i.e., if the defendant effectively owns or hired the machine or intended to invade the patentee's right).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the substance of the contract (real vs colorable). If evidence permits inference that the defendant owned, partly owned, or hired the machine (or intended to invade the patent), liability can follow (Keplinger v. De Young). Courts examine facts to see whether the transaction was a device to evade the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard for injunctions where answer under oath exists
rubrics_metrics.description: When a defendant files an answer under oath denying use, something more than the unsupported affidavit of a single witness is required to overcome that sworn answer and obtain an injunction; courts will require sufficient evidence to rebut the sworn denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In preliminary equity relief (injunction) contexts, treat a defendant's sworn answer as strong evidence; plaintiffs need more than a lone, vague affidavit to overcome it (Carpenter v. Prov. Wash. Ins. Co. and related discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of a patented machine: must be sale of complete machine with right to use
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale that constitutes infringement must be of a complete patented machine 'for use as a machine' with the right, express or implied, of using it in the manner secured by the patent; sale of mere materials (separate or combined) is not, by itself, an infringing 'sale.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish sale of materials from tortious sale of a machine with a right to use. A sheriff's sale of materials of a patented machine ordinarily is not infringement (Sawin v. Guild); the officer selling materials is not responsible unless he guarantees a right to use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of products made by a patented machine/process is generally not infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale of articles produced by a patented machine or by a patented process (the product) is not an infringement of the patent right in the machine/process; the patent protects the thing patented, not the produced product, except where the seller is connected with the use of the patented thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purchasers and resellers of products made by someone else using a patented machine are not normally liable; liability attaches only if the seller is in some manner connected with or benefits from the unlawful use of the patented machine (Boyd v. Brown, Keplinger discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendor connected to use can be enjoined even for out-of-jurisdiction use
rubrics_metrics.description: If the person who sells the product is connected with the use of the patented machine, he is responsible as for an infringement and may be enjoined, and a court of equity having jurisdiction of the person may enjoin him even though the machine is used beyond the court's territorial jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for ownership, hiring, control, or profit nexus between vendor and the infringing use. Connection suffices to support equitable relief against the vendor (Boyd v. McAlpin and commentary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of exclusive territorial rights does not prevent assignee from selling products elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of an exclusive right to use a machine and to vend the same to others for use within a specified territory authorizes the assignee to vend articles manufactured by such machine elsewhere, out of that territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Territorial assignments of rights to use/vend the machine do not necessarily forbid the assignee from selling the manufactured articles outside the assigned territory; courts have so held (citation to Supreme Court decision noted in text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents for manufacture or composition: infringement by making/using/selling the thing itself
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for a 'manufacture' or a 'composition of matter' is infringed by the same acts: making, using, or selling the thing itself — i.e., the vendible/tangible product is protected and infringement occurs when the product itself is made/used/sold without authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the statutory verbs directly to the patented article (manufacture/composition) — the same modes of infringement (make/use/sell) apply as for machines, but directed at the thing patented (the product) rather than an apparatus.
